title: The mobile visit for a restaurant group
metaTitle: The mobile visit for a restaurant group
excerpt: Most guests will judge a restaurant group on a phone. The first screen still has to show the room, one dish, and a way to the menu or a table.
alt: A two-lane road through red rock, with a single car far ahead and a mountain at the end, a long approach that only helps if the destination stays visible.
caption: A long road and one clear destination. The phone screen needs that kind of clarity. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What must the first phone screen contain?
faqs.answer: A recognizable room or one dish, the restaurant's name, and a way to see the menu or book a table. Hours or the neighborhood should be in that same glance. If a desktop film pushed those facts below the fold, the phone page is unfinished.

faqs.question: Should the desktop design lead?
faqs.answer: Design the phone first for this guest, then let the wide screen add room. A cinematic desktop header that becomes a logo animation on a phone has let the wrong device decide. Wide screens can have more margin. They should not tell a different story.

faqs.question: How do we know the phone visit works?
faqs.answer: Stand outside and try to choose a restaurant, open its menu, and start a booking with one thumb. The page should load the room quickly and should not jump as images arrive. If you need a laptop to tell the rooms apart, the visit is still a desktop visit.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A restaurant group mobile website is the version most guests will actually judge. They are deciding where to go tonight, on a phone, often outside. The first screen still has to show the room and one dish, and a way to see the menu or book a table. Do not let the desktop composition decide the phone page.

If the wide layout needs a film before the room makes sense, the phone will not wait. It will get a crop and a thumb. Design for that.

## The guest is on a phone

Assume glare, one hand, and a group chat. Nielsen Norman Group's research on [how long people stay on web pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) found that the first 10 seconds decide whether people stay, and that a clear value proposition in those seconds earns a longer look. On a phone those seconds are one screen.

The value proposition is a room they might sit in, a dish, and a way to act. Not a logo drawing itself. Not a manifesto in tiny type. If the sentence does not fit, shorten it. Do not tuck the hours under the animation.

[web.dev's Web Vitals](https://web.dev/articles/vitals) ask you to judge experience at the 75th percentile, on mobile and on desktop. A page that feels instant on the office display and late on a phone has not passed. Largest Contentful Paint should occur within 2.5 seconds. Interaction to Next Paint should be 200 milliseconds or less. Cumulative Layout Shift should be 0.1 or less. Hold the hero, the menu, and the booking link to those numbers.

Put a phone on the table in every review. A stakeholder who only looks at a laptop will approve the wrong crop, and the guest will be the one who finds out.

## The first screen, specified

Write the first screen before anyone opens a layout.

- One photograph of the room or one dish, cropped so it survives a phone width.
- The restaurant name, the neighborhood, and hours as text.
- Menu and Book a table, aimed at that restaurant.
- The other rooms as names, not as a mystery grid.

That is the screen. A film can sit later, muted, captioned, skippable. A logo animation does not belong on it at all.

Test the crop by covering the sides of the desktop frame. If the dish or the seats disappear, art-direct a separate crop. The caption must match what the phone shows. Do not describe a booth the crop has removed.

Type has to be readable without pinch-zoom. Hours in pale type over a dark plate will be missed, and a missed hour is a bad walk. Put hours on a solid ground. The buttons need space a thumb can hit. A sticky header that eats a third of the screen is how the dish falls away. Keep the header short: the room name and Book.

## Desktop is the wrong master

Keep the wide composition for wide screens. Do not let it set the order of the content. Phone order is image, name, hours, menu, book, then the other rooms. Desktop can place type beside the image. It should not introduce a film the phone then inherits as a blocker.

Beware hover effects. Phones do not hover. If the restaurant name appears only when a cursor arrives, the mobile visit is a silent gallery. Put the name in the page.

Beware a horizontal swipe as the only way to see three rooms. Stack the names. A swipe can be extra. It cannot be the index.

Beware a video header that autoplays. It costs data, it delays the hours, and it often fails to show a chair until the guest has left. If you keep a film, start it after the facts, on a gesture.

Review desktop second. Ask whether the wide screen keeps the same facts with more comfort. If desktop adds a manifesto above the rooms, delete it in both layouts. Do not maintain two arguments.

## Hours, address, menu, book

These four have to work with a thumb. Hours as text, including the closure that would waste a trip. Address as text a guest can copy into a map, not only a pin that fails to load. Menu as a page that scrolls, with prices, not a PDF you have not tested. Book as a link that already knows the venue.

Test each room, not only the flagship. The second restaurant is where the link usually points at the first. That is a mobile bug and a floor bug. Fix the link.

The menu must open. Pinching a PDF in a parking lot is how bookings die. If you are stuck with a PDF this week, test it on the phone you expect guests to use, and plan the HTML menu. Prices have to be readable. A menu that hides numbers forces the guest back to the host you were trying not to call.

Do not cover this screen with a newsletter modal, a cookie wall that hides the dish, or an awards popup. The guest needed a table. Give them the table.

### A walk you take before service

Leave the office. Load the site on a phone that is not on the studio Wi-Fi. Pick a room. Read the hours. Open the menu. Start a booking and cancel before you confirm, unless you are on a test system. Then do the next room.

Note where the page is blank, where the name is missing, and where the widget asks you to choose the restaurant again. Those notes are the punch list. Fix crops and links before you add motion. Most mobile failures for a restaurant group are a late image, a PDF, and a booking link that forgot the venue.

Check a closed day on purpose. The site should say the room is closed before the guest taps Book. If the widget is the only one who knows, the page is lying by omission. Put the sentence in HTML.

If the first screen is still a logo animation when you look up from the sidewalk, delete the animation before the next sitting. You do not need a redesign to do that. You need the room in the first paint. Book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min) if you want that pass done with a studio that will hold the phone to the same standard as the desktop. Bring the current homepage on your own phone. Hanabi designs and builds. The half hour should end with the first screen written down: room, dish, hours, menu, book.

## Menus that open, links that remember

The photograph can be perfect and the visit can still fail on the next tap. The menu has to open on the phone as text, with prices large enough to read on the sidewalk. A PDF that asks the guest to download, rotate, and pinch is a closed door. If the PDF is all you have tonight, test it before service and put the hours in HTML beside it so the file is not the only source of truth.

The booking link has to remember which restaurant the guest was looking at. Test this from each room's first screen, not from a spreadsheet of URLs in the office. A link that dumps everyone into the flagship will fill one book and empty the others. That is a content bug. Fix it in the button, not with a paragraph that says "please select your venue."

Address and hours sit in the same glance as the picture. Copy the address as text. Say the closed day in a sentence. A map tile can follow. It cannot be the only way to know the suburb. When the picture, the hours, and the correct link agree, the phone visit is doing the job the desktop film was pretending to do.

Do this check on the day you change a menu, not only at launch. A new price in a PDF that the phone cannot open is a silent change. A new dish photographed and never captioned is a silent change too. The mobile visit is a habit. Someone on the floor should be able to correct hours without a designer, and the button should still point at the right book afterward. If fixing Tuesday requires a new export of the entire hero, the page was built as a poster. Rebuild that bit as text. Guests forgive a plain sentence. They do not forgive a beautiful page that sent them across town on a closed Monday. Read the first screen aloud on the pavement once a month. If you stumble, the guest will leave. The sentence you can say without looking is the sentence the phone should show.

## What they do when they are ready

A clear first screen creates a reply that is not always a booking widget. A private room, a buyout, a question about a cake. If that path is a ten-field form, the phone visit ends in a shrug even after the dish did its work.

The next piece is [a contact path for a restaurant group](/blog/a-contact-path-for-a-restaurant-group). Design it for the same thumb. The room got their attention. The path has to be as clear as the hours.
